title: Romans 10:14–21
context: Paul traces the chain that leads to salvation: sending, preaching, hearing, believing, and calling. Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ. Israel has heard, yet many have not obeyed, while Gentiles who were not seeking God have found him. The section ends with God holding out his hands all day long to a disobedient people. Arminian readers find here a sincere offer that Israel refused; Reformed readers agree the offer was sincere and see God’s purpose behind both the hearing and the believing.

verses.text: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?
verses.arminianNotes: Paul asks how people can call on one they have not believed, believe in one they have not heard, or hear without a preacher. Arminian readers see the necessity of preaching for faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the ordinary means God uses to bring his people to faith.

verses.text: And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!”
verses.arminianNotes: Preachers must be sent, and their feet are beautiful. Both traditions see mission as essential to the church’s life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God sending preachers as part of his plan to gather his people.

verses.text: But they didn’t all listen to the glad news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our report?”
verses.arminianNotes: Not all obeyed the gospel; Isaiah asked who had believed the report. Arminian readers see that the gospel can be heard and refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see that hearing alone does not produce faith; the Spirit must open the heart.

verses.text: So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
verses.arminianNotes: Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ. Arminian readers see faith as the response to God’s word, enabled by grace that accompanies the message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word as the instrument through which the Spirit creates faith.
verses.keyContrast: Both agree that faith comes through hearing God’s word. Arminian readers see grace accompanying the word that enables a response. Reformed readers see the Spirit using the word to create faith in the elect.

verses.text: But I say, didn’t they hear? Yes, most certainly, “Their sound went out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.”
verses.arminianNotes: Israel has heard: their voice has gone out to all the earth. Arminian readers see that Israel’s failure was not for lack of opportunity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Israel’s accountability for rejecting a message it truly heard.

verses.text: But I ask, didn’t Israel know? First Moses says, “I will provoke you to jealousy with that which is no nation. I will make you angry with a nation void of understanding.”
verses.arminianNotes: Moses foretold that God would provoke Israel to jealousy by a people who were not a nation. Both traditions see the inclusion of Gentiles as part of God’s plan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s plan to use the Gentiles’ salvation for Israel’s good.

verses.text: Isaiah is very bold and says, “I was found by those who didn’t seek me. I was revealed to those who didn’t ask for me.”
verses.arminianNotes: God was found by those who did not seek him. Arminian readers see God taking the initiative to reach the Gentiles.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see sovereign grace: God found people who were not seeking him.

verses.text: But about Israel he says, “All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”
verses.arminianNotes: All day long God stretched out his hands to a disobedient and contrary people. Arminian readers see a sincere and persistent offer that Israel resisted, showing that God’s grace can be refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sincere appeal and Israel’s culpable refusal. They hold that God’s outstretched hands express his genuine desire, while his electing purpose explains why some respond.
verses.keyContrast: Both see God’s sincere appeal to Israel. Arminian readers see grace extended and resisted. Reformed readers affirm the sincerity of the appeal and Israel’s guilt while holding that God’s election explains who responds.
